1. The Problem

* Parallelizable vs. Fixed Parts: In the 343 µs unfiltered query, 170 µs is the fixed transport/pipe floor, and ~60 µs is serial JSON parsing and response encoding. Filtered queries have only 84 µs above the transport floor, and dictionary filtering leaves only ~1,000 candidate rows (~12 µs scan). 2. The Mechanism

* Work Division: For unfiltered TopK, partition the 10,000 row slots into two equal slices: Main thread scans

```
[0,N/2)[0,N/2)
```

```
[N/2,N)[N/2,N)
```

* Coordination & Merging: A single persistent worker thread is spawned at startup. Main thread posts query parameters, signals the worker, and scans its slice. ```

retrospective.content:
* Correction of Initial Misconceptions: Early in the project, I incorrectly assumed ranking favored the earliest submission time, and that there were two separate coding tasks. I formally clarify this: the tiebreaker is a single from-scratch MiniVectorDB evaluated post-deadline on two distinct 40-point tracks (Performance Score

```
EE
```

 and Agent Collaboration Rubric).

* Algorithmic Evolution & Trade-off Reflection:
   * Why K-means IVF failed on

```
σ=0.5σ=0.5
```

: In 128-dimensional space, higher cluster dispersion causes points to become nearly equidistant to all centroids, collapsing the triangle-inequality lower bound and preventing pruning.

   * Why SQ8 succeeded globally: SQ8 operates coordinate-wise per vector. By quantizing coordinates to 8 bits and applying a provable mathematical lower bound, it removes memory bus bottlenecks on ANY data distribution while preserving exact Recall=1.0.

Checked against measurements. The correction matches the record (c1, c3) and the rules. On sigma 0.5 the conclusion holds, the mechanism needs one change: a list can be skipped only when |q - c| exceeds its radius plus the K-th distance; at sigma 0.5 the nearest other centre is 9.76 away against 5.57 for the own one, so points are not equidistant, but radius 6.65 plus the 10th distance 7.21 exceed 9.76 and no list is ruled out (e54, e44). On SQ8: exact on any data and it reads a quarter of the bytes, so it helped on all four measured shapes (e44), but on near-duplicate rows it prunes nothing and is about 30% slower than no codes (e54).

limitations: Stage timings (e35, e39-e41) come from a scratch program outside the repository, on a machine shared with an unrelated long-running job (load average 3-5); they guided decisions, and the before/after comparisons use bench.py (e43, e44).
The scratch probe assigns categories as id % 10, a regular stride the hardware prefetcher follows, so its filtered timings favour the unpermuted slot order; bench.py draws categories at random.

An idle container on this machine already reports memory.peak 5.11 MiB before any statement (e45), so container-level M of the write phase cannot show the 2.1 MiB measured outside Docker; the grader's runtime may differ.
Clustered benchmark data (bench.py --clusters) is a synthetic Gaussian mixture chosen by the agent; the task's own data distribution was not published at the time of writing.
The cost of the k-means cap (e53) was measured on synthetic clustered data at 100,000 rows; the hidden data sizes, distribution and time limits are unpublished.
Benchmarks ran on one desktop machine (i5-9400F, NVMe ext4), mostly outside Docker with I/O from /proc/<pid>/io; inside Docker (e23) io.stat gave the same byte counts.
The reference model was written from the same reading of the task as the engine, so it finds implementation bugs but cannot catch a shared misreading of the rules.

Filter pushdown and the benchmark cover one filter shape (string equality over 10 categories); other conditions take the generic per-row path, and SELECT without ORDER BY still walks the primary-key index.
